rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report supports the reading that completing the count means completing the month of Ramadan.
rows.anchor: الرواية تدل على ما قدمناه أن ظاهر التكميل تكميل شهر رمضان

rows.speaker: بعض أصحابنا
rows.claim: A report in al-Barqī’s Maḥāsin glosses takbīr as magnification and guidance as wilāya.
rows.anchor: وفي محاسن البرقي عن بعض أصحابنا رفعه في قوله ولتكبروا الله على ما هداكم قال التكبير التعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He treats guidance as wilāya as an application or identification of an instance, possibly taʾwīl; reports also identify ease with wilāya and hardship with opposition and the rule of God’s enemies.
rows.anchor: والهداية الولاية من باب الجري وبيان المصداق ويمكن أن يكون من قبيل ما يسمى تأويلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some reports identify ease with wilāya and hardship with opposition to it and the authority of God’s enemies.
rows.anchor: في بعض الروايات أن اليسر هو الولاية، والعسر الخلاف

words: شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أُنزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلْقُرْءَانُ
rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Asked how the Qur’an was revealed in Ramadan though its descent spanned twenty years, al-Ṣādiq says it descended all at once to al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr, then over twenty years.
rows.anchor: نزل القرآن جملة واحدة في شهر رمضان إلى البيت المعمور ثم نزل في طول عشرين سنة

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet’s chronology says the Suḥuf came on Ramadan’s first night, Torah on the sixth, Zabūr on the eighteenth, and Qur’an on the twenty-third.
rows.anchor: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes that al-Suyūṭī also transmits the Prophet’s revelation chronology through several routes from Wāʾila b. al-Asqaʿ.
rows.anchor: رواه السيوطي في الدر المنثور بعدة طرق عن وائلة بن الأسقع عن النبي

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Asked whether the Night of Decree occurred once or recurs annually, al-Ṣādiq answers that if it were removed, the Qur’an would be removed.
rows.anchor: عن يعقوب قال سمعت رجلا يسأل أبا عبد الله عن ليلة القدر فقال أخبرني عن ليلة القدر كانت أو تكون في كل سنة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies Ramadan, the blessed night, and the Night of Decree as the same night: the Qur’an descended whole to al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr, then piecemeal to Muhammad in commands, prohibitions, and wars.
rows.anchor: وفي الدر المنثور عن ابن عباس، قال شهر رمضان والليلة المباركة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the same account of the Qur’an’s whole descent to al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr is also narrated from Saʿīd b. Jubayr.
rows.anchor: وروي هذا المعنى عن غيره أيضا كسعيد بن جبير

words: شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أُنزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلْقُرْءَانُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited Qur’anic evidence includes al-Tur’s references to an inscribed book, al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr, and the raised ceiling.
rows.anchor: وكتاب مسطور في رق منشور والبيت المعمور

words: شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أُنزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلْقُرْءَانُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited passages are mostly clear, but reading the star positions as the first heaven and the Qur’an’s location there is obscure; al-Wāqiʿa does not clearly prove it.
rows.anchor: وجميع ذلك ظاهر إلا ما ذكره في مواقع

rows.speaker: أهل البيت
rows.claim: Reports from the Prophet’s Household place al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr in heaven.
rows.anchor: وقد ورد من طرق أهل البيت أن البيت المعمور في السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadith, like the Qur’an, includes clear and ambiguous material; allusion and symbol are common for realities such as the Tablet, Pen, veils, heaven, al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr, and the sealed sea, so interpretation needs contextual clues.
rows.anchor: أن الحديث كمثل القرآن في اشتماله على المحكم والمتشابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The placement of the rule after the command to depart from ʿArafāt, with thumma, marks order of mention and works as a correction: the required departure is from ʿArafāt, not Muzdalifa.
rows.anchor: بثم الدالة على التأخير اعتبار للترتيب الذكري

words: ثُمَّ أَفِيضُوا۟ مِنْ حَيْثُ أَفَاضَ ٱلنَّاسُ
rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some exegetes say the two verses were transposed in composition: the command to depart from where people depart should precede the command to depart from ʿArafāt.
rows.anchor: وربما قيل إن في الآيتين تقديما وتأخيرا في التأليف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After pilgrimage rites, worshippers are urged to remember God as they remember their fathers, or more intensely, because God’s gift of guidance gives them a greater claim than their parents.
rows.anchor: بأن يذكره الناسك كذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In pre-Islamic practice, Arabs stayed for a time at Minā after pilgrimage and boasted of their forefathers in verse and prose; God replaced this with remembrance of Him.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل إن العرب كانت في الجاهلية إذا فرغت من الحج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here aw in “or more intensely” signals correction and means “rather.”
rows.anchor: وأو في قوله أو أشد ذكرا للإضراب فتفيد معنى بل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembrance can be intense in quality as well as abundant in quantity.
rows.anchor: وقد وصف الذكر بالشدة وهو أمر يقبل الشدة في الكيفية كما يقبل الكثرة في الكمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr is not limited to spoken words: speech reports a presence of the heart.
rows.anchor: ليس مقصورا في اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an illustrates abundant remembrance across circumstances with commands and descriptions of remembering God often, and remembering Him standing, sitting, and lying down.
rows.anchor: الذين يذكرون الله قياما وقعودا وعلى جنوبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because finishing pilgrimage invites distraction and forgetfulness of God, the verse fittingly calls for intense remembrance rather than simply abundant remembrance.
rows.anchor: المورد المستفاد من قوله تعالى

words: فَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَقُولُ رَبَّنَآ ءَاتِنَا فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The division of people into those who seek worldly life and those who seek God’s approval follows from the command to remember Him.
rows.anchor: فاذكروا الله كذكركم آباءكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “People” is generic: one group, including unbelievers, pursues worldly status and has no concern for the afterlife; the other seeks only what God approves, in either life, and has an afterlife share.
rows.anchor: فالمراد به أفراد الإنسان أعم من الكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s “saying” and supplication describe an inward orientation or state, not necessarily literal spoken words.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا فالمراد بالقول والدعاء ما هو سؤال بلسان الحال دون المقال

words: وَمَا لَهُۥ فِى ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ مِنْ خَلَٰقٍ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly seeker accepts whatever pleases his desire as good, while the seeker of God’s approval distinguishes good from evil in both lives and asks only for good.
rows.anchor: لا يقيده بأن يكون حسنا عند الله سبحانه

words: وَمَا لَهُۥ فِى ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ مِنْ خَلَٰقٍ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast between having no afterlife share and receiving a share for one’s deeds shows that the first group’s works are nullified, unlike the second’s.
rows.anchor: وما له في الآخرة من خلاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Swift in reckoning” is a divine name whose scope includes both worlds: God continually repays each servant in keeping with each deed.
rows.anchor: اسم من أسماء الله الحسنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage urges remembrance: worldly-only seekers have no afterlife share, God-oriented seekers do, and God swiftly grants what His servant seeks; be among those with a share.
rows.anchor: فالمحصل من معنى قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The numbered days are the three Tashrīq days, the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth of Dhū al-Ḥijja; their placement after pilgrimage rites and the two-day departure support this, as do reports.
rows.anchor: الأيام المعدودات هي أيام التشريق وهي اليوم الحادي عشر والثاني عشر والثالث عشر من ذي الحجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about departing in two days presupposes three days: one day for departure and two days in which to hasten away.
rows.anchor: فإن التعجل في يومين إنما يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports also identify the numbered days as the three Tashrīq days.
rows.anchor: وقد فسرت في الروايات بذلك أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā in both clauses is lā li-l-jins, denying sin categorically; if the point were merely permission to leave early or late, the denial would need that qualification.
rows.anchor: لا نافية للجنس فقوله { لا إثم عليه }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse means a pilgrim who completes the pilgrimage is forgiven whether departing early or staying, rather than merely being given a choice between those timings.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى أن من أتم عمل الحج فهو مغفور لا ذنب له سواء تعجل في يومين أو تأخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “For whoever is Godfearing” does not syntactically qualify early or late departure; if it did, the expected wording would be “upon whoever is Godfearing.”
rows.anchor: فليس بيانا للتعجل والتأخر وإلا لكان حق الكلام أن يقال على من اتقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ruling applies to those who avoid the prohibited acts of pilgrimage, especially some or all ihrām restrictions; one who does not must remain at Minā and remember God on the numbered days.
rows.anchor: أن الحكم إنما هو لمن اتقى تروك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some reports from the Imams of the Prophet’s Household support this interpretation of the Godfearing qualifier.
rows.anchor: وقد ورد هذا المعنى في بعض ما روي عن أئمه أهل البيت عليهم السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khamr linguistically means any liquid made to intoxicate; its root sense is covering, since it veils the mind and its ability to distinguish good from evil.
rows.anchor: الخمر على ما يستفاد من اللغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The related words khimār, khammartu, and akhmartu refer respectively to a woman’s head covering, covering a vessel, and putting yeast into dough to make it rise.
rows.anchor: ويقال لما تغطي به المرأة رأسها الخمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs originally knew wine made from grapes, dates, and barley; later varieties multiplied and all intoxicating kinds, across levels of potency, are khamr.
rows.anchor: وقد كانت العرب لا تعرف من أقسامه إلا الخمر المعمول من العنب والتمر والشعير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maysir means gambling and yāsir means gambler; its root connotes ease because it acquires another’s property without the toil of earning.
rows.anchor: والميسر لغة هو القمار ويسمى المقامر ياسرا والأصل في معناه السهولة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A common Arabian form of gambling used arrows or lots to divide a slaughtered camel into twenty-eight shares among ten men; seven winning arrows awarded one to seven shares, while three losing arrows had no share and their holders paid the camel’s cost.
rows.anchor: وهو الضرب بالقداح وهي السهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ten arrows were al-fadhdh, al-tawʾam, al-raqīb, al-ḥils, al-nāfis, al-musbِل, al-muʿallā, al-manīḥ, al-sanīḥ, and al-raghd; the first seven drew assigned shares and the last three drew none.
rows.anchor: وهي الفذ، والتوأم، والرقيب، والحلس، والنافس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reading has kathīr, “much sin,” with thāʾ instead of the written reading kabīr, “great sin.”
rows.anchor: وقرىء إثم كثير بالثاء المثلثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ithm is close to sin and describes a condition in an act or mind that slows a person from attaining good; wine and gambling have this quality.
rows.anchor: والإثم يقارب الذنب وما يشبهه معنى وهو حال في الشيء أو في العقل يبطئ الإنسان عن نيل الخيرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wine causes grave medical harms to the stomach, intestines, liver, lungs, nerves, arteries, heart, and senses, as physicians’ writings and statistics document.
rows.anchor: مضراته الطبية وآثاره السيئة في المعدة والأمعاء والكبد والرئة وسلسلة الأعصاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wine degrades character and leads to obscenity, violence, crimes, murder, divulging secrets, violating rights, and destroying human laws of life, especially protection of honor, life, and property.
rows.anchor: وأما مضراته الخلقية من تشويه الخلق وتأديته الإنسان إلى الفحش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The impairment of perception and intellect during intoxication and afterward is undeniable, is wine’s greatest sin and corruption, and generates its other corruptions.
rows.anchor: وأما مضرته في الإدراك وسلبه العقل وتصرفه الغير المنتظم في أفكار الإنسان وتغييره مجرى الإدراك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic law protects sound reason and strongly forbids what disables it, including wine, gambling, fraud, and lies; wine and falsehood especially defeat reason’s governance.
rows.anchor: والشريعة الإسلامية كما مرت إليه الإشارة وضعت أساس أحكامها على التحفظ على العقل السليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Actions and policies built on intoxication and lies threaten humanity and undermine happiness; a law grounded in reason and barring desire that corrupts it is a source of honor.
rows.anchor: فهذه الأعمال أعني الأعمال المبطلة لحكومة العقل وعلى رأسها السياسات المبتنية على السكر والكذب هي التي تهدد الإنسانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because sensual habits spread quickly and are hard to abandon, God legislates gradually and gently; wine prohibition is one example of that progressive approach.
rows.anchor: ولذلك أن الله سبحانه شرع فيهم ما شرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meccan 16:67 mentions intoxicating drink and good provision; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats this as an early, non-explicit stage in wine’s gradual prohibition.
rows.anchor: ومن ثمرات النخيل والأعناب تتخذون منه سكرا ورزقا حسنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Medinan 4:43 bars drinking or drunkenness at prayer, limiting it at the best time and place; it precedes al-Baqara and al-Māʾida, since a specific ban after a universal one would reverse the gradual move from ease to severity.
rows.anchor: والآية مدنية وهي تمنع الناس بعض المنع عن الشرب والسكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqara 2:219 came after 4:43 and establishes prohibition by decisively calling wine a great sin, against the background of the earlier Meccan prohibition of sin.
rows.anchor: ثم نزلت آية البقرة أعني قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some exegetes argue that this verse is not explicit in prohibition: sin means harm, and an item with both harm and benefit is not thereby forbidden; they say Companions differed, some abstaining and others continuing while avoiding harm, until al-Māʾida’s explicit ban.
rows.anchor: فساد ما ذكره بعض المفسرين أن آية البقرة ما كانت صريحة في الحرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: First, sin does not simply mean harm; that definition fails for Qur’anic uses of ithm concerning associating partners, a sinful heart, liability for another’s sin, and acquired sins.
rows.anchor: أما أولا فإنه أخذ الإثم بمعنى الضرر مطلقا وليس الإثم هو الضرر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kibr compares to size what abundance compares to number; greatness and smallness are relational opposites first understood physically, then extended metaphorically to abstract matters.
rows.anchor: وأما الكبر فهو في الأحجام بمنزلة الكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author points to shirk as another sin called great, using the Qur’an’s description in 4:48 when arguing that wine’s sin is especially grave.
rows.anchor: ومن يشرك بالله فقد افترى إثما عظيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not explain the ruling merely by harm; even on that assumption, it explicitly says the sin outweighs the benefit, so appeal to independent Companion reasoning contradicts the text.
rows.anchor: وأما ثانيا فإن الآية لم تعلل الحكم بالضرر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if 2:219 alone were insufficient to establish prohibition, its explicit naming of sin follows 7:33’s earlier general prohibition; wine is a complete instance of great sin.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية قيدت الإثم بالكبر ولا يبقى مع ذلك ريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an calls killing, concealing testimony, and false accusation sin, but does not call these great sins; it calls wine’s sin great and describes shirk as a great sin.
rows.anchor: وقد وصف القرآن القتل وكتمان الشهادة والافتراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After al-Baqara, al-Māʾida 5:90–91 calls wine and gambling satanic pollution and commands avoidance; its closing question shows Muslims had not fully ceased drinking before then.
rows.anchor: وذيل الكلام يدل على أن المسلمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gambling’s social harms and its destruction of the structure of life are visible directly; the author defers fuller discussion to Sūrat al-Māʾida.
rows.anchor: وأما الميسر فمفاسده الاجتماعية وهدمه لبنيان الحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Benefit and harm describe things sought or avoided for something else, unlike good and evil, which describe things sought or avoided for their own sake.
rows.anchor: والنفع خلاف الضرر ويطلقان على الأمور المطلوبة لغيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The benefits people seek in wine and gambling are monetary gains from sale, purchase, and work, along with amusement and pleasure.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالمنافع فيهما ما يقصده الناس بهما من الاستفادات المالية بالبيع والشرى والعمل والتفكه والتلهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although benefits is plural earlier, the comparison says benefit in the singular: plurality does not affect greatness, so the quantity of benefits is left out of the comparison.
rows.anchor: فقيل وإثمهما أكبر من نفعهما ولم يقل

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib derives ʿafw from aiming at something to take it, then notes its later senses of forgiveness, effacing traces, and moderation in spending; moderation is intended here.
rows.anchor: العفو على ما ذكره الراغب قصد الشيء لتناوله ثم أوجب لحوق العنايات المختلفة الكلامية به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intended ʿafw here is the moderate or surplus amount to spend; he adds “God knows best.”
rows.anchor: وهذا هو المقصود في المقام، والله العالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question and answer about what to spend match the earlier question answered by saying that whatever good is spent goes to parents and relatives.
rows.anchor: والكلام في مطابقة الجواب للسؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “in this world and the Hereafter” modifies “you reflect,” rather than functioning as an adverbial phrase for something else.
rows.anchor: الظرف أعني قوله تعالى { في الدنيا والآخرة }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse invites reflection on both abodes: God created this world for life and for acquiring what benefits people in the final abode, where they return for judgment on their deeds.
rows.anchor: والمعنى لعلكم تتفكرون في أمر الدارين وما يرتبط بكم من حقيقتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The invitation to reflection encompasses realities of existence, God and return, nature, society, ethics, and individual and communal life, namely all knowledge tied to human happiness and misery.
rows.anchor: حث على البحث عن حقائق الوجود ومعارف المبدأ والمعاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Qur’an commands full obedience to God and His Messenger, it does not approve receiving its rulings and teachings through blind rigidity without thought and reason.
rows.anchor: غير أنه لا يرضى أن تؤخذ الأحكام والمعارف التي يعطيها على العمى والجمود المحض من غير تفكر وتعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabyīn here means uncovering the reasons behind rulings and clarifying the foundations of teachings and knowledge.
rows.anchor: وكأن المراد بالتبيين هو الكشف عن علل الأحكام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allowing association with orphans and adding that God could have burdened people signals relief from an earlier strictness that had unsettled Muslims and prompted their question.
rows.anchor: في الآية إشعار بل دلالة على نوع من التخفيف والتسهيل حيث أجازت المخالطة لليتامى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stern earlier warnings against consuming orphans’ wealth in 4:10 and 4:2 support the inference that this verse followed the verses of Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.
rows.anchor: كقوله تعالى إن الذين يأكلون أموال اليتامى ظلما إنما يأكلون في بطونهم نارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite “reform” denotes a particular kind, not every purported reform: what God approves is actual reform, not merely an outward appearance.
rows.anchor: حيث نكر الإصلاح دلالة على أن المرضي عند الله سبحانه نوع من الإصلاح لا كل إصلاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s closing statement that God knows the corrupter and reformer supports reading reform as genuine rather than merely apparent.
rows.anchor: ويشعر به قوله تعالى ذيلا والله يعلم المفسد من المصلح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling orphans fellow believers signals equality among believers by erasing distinctions that enable domination and injustice; this balances weak orphans with guardians, the poor with the rich, and the deficient with the complete.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى المساواة المجعولة بين المؤمنين جميعا بإلغاء جميع الصفات المميزة
